title: Pacific Atlantic Water Flow
description: Reverse-flood DFS from each ocean's edges; intersect the two reach-sets to find cells that drain to both oceans. O(R*C).

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down the inputs.
sections.say:
"Let me make sure I have this right: I get a 2D matrix `heights` representing land elevations. The Pacific touches the top and left edges; the Atlantic touches the bottom and right. Water flows from a cell to a 4-neighbor only if the neighbor's height is ≤ the current cell's. I return all cells whose water can reach BOTH oceans."

Then a few quick clarifying questions:
• Flow rule — '≤' (water flows to equal-or-lower), confirmed? Some variants use strict '<'.
• Heights — non-negative integers? Could they be zero? Negative?
• Edge ownership — corners (top-left etc.) belong to BOTH oceans automatically, right? (Pacific = top OR left; Atlantic = bottom OR right; corners satisfy both.)
• Output order — does the problem expect a specific ordering? (LeetCode accepts any; row-major is natural.)
• Grid dimensions — guaranteed at least 1x1?
sections.why: The '≤ vs <' rule is the load-bearing clarification — it determines whether equal-height plateaus drain freely (≤, the LeetCode default) or block flow entirely (<). Get this wrong and your algorithm gives wrong answers on the most common edge case (flat regions). The corner question is a sanity check: the four corners ALWAYS reach both oceans regardless of height because they sit on both edges. Confirming this up front prevents a separate special-case branch — the algorithm handles it naturally because both DFS frontiers start from those cells.

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name the naive approach to motivate the reversal trick.
sections.say:
"The obvious brute force is: for every cell `(r, c)`, run a flood-fill that follows the natural water-flow rule (move to ≤-height neighbors), and check whether the flood reaches BOTH a Pacific edge cell AND an Atlantic edge cell. That's O(R·C) cells, each launching a flood that could visit up to O(R·C) cells, total O(R²·C²). For a 100x100 grid that's 10⁸ operations — borderline. For 200x200 it's 1.6·10⁹ — too slow.

The specific waste: cells near the middle of the grid get re-visited by EVERY flood that passes through them. Cell (50, 50) might be visited by all 10000 floods. The fix is to invert the direction — instead of asking 'from each cell, can I reach both oceans?', ask 'from each ocean, which cells can drain into it?' Then the answer is the intersection."
sections.why: Naming the per-cell flood as O(R²·C²) is the critical motivation. It frames the next section's reversal as 'I'm restructuring to avoid the per-cell waste' rather than 'I'm using a clever trick I memorized'. The reframing also makes the answer feel inevitable — once you see that the work is dominated by repeatedly visiting middle cells, the move to 'visit each cell once per ocean' (O(R·C) total) is the obvious fix. The brute force isn't a strawman — it's literally what most candidates try first.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern
sections.prompt: What signal in the problem points to reverse-direction multi-source flood?
sections.say:
"Here's the trick — and it's the whole problem: instead of running a forward flood from every cell asking 'can I reach both oceans?', flip the question and run a REVERSE flood FROM each ocean asking 'which cells can drain INTO me?'

Reverse flow means: if water naturally flows DOWNHILL (height decreasing or equal), I walk UPHILL (height increasing or equal) from the ocean edge. So from an edge cell at height h, I can step to a neighbor only if the neighbor's height is ≥ h. Mathematically: a cell C can reach the ocean iff the ocean can climb to C in reverse — same set of cells, different walking direction.

The algorithm:
1. Initialize two visited matrices, `pac` (Pacific reachable) and `atl` (Atlantic reachable), both R·C booleans.
2. For every cell on the top row and left column, run a DFS that fills `pac` with everything reachable via ≥-height moves. Use `prev = -Infinity` to seed — that lets the edge cell itself enter.
3. Same for bottom row and right column, filling `atl`.
4. The answer is the intersection: every cell where `pac[r][c] && atl[r][c]`.

Why this is O(R·C) and not O(R²·C²): each cell is visited at most ONCE per ocean (gated by its visited matrix), so each cell is touched at most twice across the entire algorithm. The total work is 2·R·C visits plus the linear iteration to collect the intersection.

The pattern name: 'reverse multi-source BFS/DFS'. Multi-source because you seed from EVERY edge cell (not just one); reverse because you walk against the flow. Same shape shows up in Walls and Gates (multi-source BFS from gates) and 01-Matrix (multi-source BFS from 0s)."
sections.why: This is the section where the conversation lives or dies. The reverse-direction insight is the WHOLE problem; if you can't articulate why we flip, you're just reciting code. The 'water flowing downhill from C to ocean iff ocean climbing uphill to C' equivalence is the mathematical justification — and it's worth stating in those exact words because it makes the reversal feel like a derivation rather than a magic trick. The complexity argument ('each cell visited at most twice total') is what justifies the work. Naming the pattern as 'multi-source reverse BFS/DFS' and cross-referencing Walls and Gates and 01-Matrix proves you see the template, not just this problem.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a few inputs to confirm the model before writing the loop.
sections.intro: "Let me trace through a couple of cases to make sure my model is right." Three inputs cover the interesting behaviors — the classic LeetCode example (multiple cells reach both oceans), an all-equal flat grid (every cell drains everywhere), and a single cell (degenerate both-corners case).

examples.note: Classic LeetCode 417 case. Pacific DFS from top row + left col; Atlantic DFS from bottom row + right col; intersect.
examples.trace:
Pacific seed (top row + left col):
  dfs(0,0,pac,-Inf): h=1 → mark. neighbors: (1,0) h=3≥1 mark, (0,1) h=2≥1 mark, ...
  dfs(0,4,pac,-Inf): h=5 → mark. (1,4) h=4<5 STOP. (0,3) h=3<5 STOP.
  ... continues from each top-row + left-col cell
  Final pac: top-left region + ridges along the left edge + cells reachable by climbing from there

Atlantic seed (bottom row + right col):
  dfs(4,4,atl,-Inf): h=4 → mark. (4,3) h=2<4 STOP. (3,4) h=5≥4 mark...
  dfs(0,4,atl,-Inf): h=5 → mark. neighbors all <5 STOP.
  ... continues from each bottom-row + right-col cell
  Final atl: bottom-right region + ridges along the right edge

Intersection (row-major scan):
  (0,4): pac=T (left-col path reaches it via climb), atl=T (it's on right edge) → include
  (1,3): pac=T, atl=T → include
  (1,4): both → include
  (2,2): both → include (it's the peak that drains both ways)
  (3,0): both → include
  (3,1): both → include
  (4,0): both → include
  output: [[0,4],[1,3],[1,4],[2,2],[3,0],[3,1],[4,0]]

examples.note: All-equal flat grid — every cell drains to every neighbor (≥ rule is satisfied trivially), so every cell reaches both oceans.
examples.trace:
Pacific DFS from (0,0),(0,1),(1,0): all four cells marked (≥-rule passes for all neighbors)
Atlantic DFS from (1,0),(1,1),(0,1): same four cells marked
Intersection: every cell
output: [[0,0],[0,1],[1,0],[1,1]]

examples.note: Single cell — it's on every edge (top, bottom, left, right) so both DFS seeds include it. Trivially in both visited matrices.
examples.trace:
Pacific DFS: dfs(0,0,pac,-Inf) → mark pac[0][0]=true
Atlantic DFS: dfs(0,0,atl,-Inf) → mark atl[0][0]=true
Intersection: pac[0][0] && atl[0][0] → include
output: [[0,0]]

sections.why: Tracing surfaces the conceptual moves that make this problem click. (1) The classic example shows the intersection is non-trivial — most cells reach ONE ocean but not both; only the 'ridge' cells that connect both watersheds appear in the output. (2) The all-flat grid is the proof that '≤' (not '<') for the natural-flow rule means '≥' (not '>') for the reverse-climb rule — if you used strict '>' for the reverse climb, flat plateaus would block flow and you'd miss obvious answers. (3) The single-cell case proves the four corners are always in the output because they're on both edges by definition — no special case needed; both DFS seeds include them.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases to mention
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Before I declare it done, let me think about edges:
• Empty grid `heights=[]` → guard with `if (!heights.length || !heights[0].length) return []`.
• Single cell `[[x]]` → both edges contain it, output is `[[0,0]]` regardless of x.
• Single row or single column → every cell is on at least the Pacific (top) AND the Atlantic (bottom for a row-of-1) edge or similar. All cells should appear in the output IF the heights allow climb in both directions. Worth tracing.
• All-equal heights → every cell reaches both oceans; output is the full grid. The ≥-rule must allow equal heights.
• All-decreasing toward one corner (e.g. heights[r][c] = max - r - c) — water naturally flows to that corner. Only the topmost-and-leftmost cells reach the Pacific freely; almost nothing reaches the Atlantic. Be sure your reverse-climb rule lets the Pacific seed reach high cells via the long uphill walk.
• Forgetting to seed from `-Infinity` — if you start the DFS with `prev = heights[r][c]`, the seed cell itself fails the ≥-check (since for the edge cell, prev IS its own height — wait, that passes — but in fact the bug is starting with no prev at all and skipping the seed cell). Using `-Infinity` as the seed `prev` is the clean idiom: the edge cell always satisfies `h ≥ -Infinity` and enters the DFS normally.
• Forgetting to maintain SEPARATE visited matrices for Pacific and Atlantic — if you share one `seen` array, the second DFS pass thinks Pacific-reached cells are already visited and never explores them. The two oceans need independent reachability tracking.
• Forgetting the intersection step — returning `pac` or `atl` alone gives 'cells reaching ONE ocean', not 'cells reaching BOTH'. The `&&` in the collection loop is the answer."
sections.why: The 'separate visited matrices' point is the second most important after the reverse-direction insight — it's a beginner bug that turns the algorithm into a totally different (and wrong) algorithm. The `-Infinity` seed trick is the elegant alternative to a per-edge special case ('mark the edge cell true, then DFS from it') — interviewers appreciate the cleaner idiom. The single-row/single-column case is the cheap sanity check: it forces every cell to be in BOTH visited matrices because every cell is on both relevant edges, and tracing it confirms your algorithm handles 'edge cells' generically.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the complexity claim?
sections.say:
"Time is O(R·C). Each cell is visited at most TWICE total — once per ocean's DFS. The visited matrices act as memoization: once a cell is marked in `pac`, the Pacific DFS will not re-enter it (the `if (seen[r][c]) return` guard short-circuits). Same for `atl`. The final collection loop is another O(R·C) scan. Total: O(R·C).

Space is O(R·C) — two visited matrices plus the recursion stack (up to R·C on a snake-shaped reachable region).

The key insight to defend against 'isn't this O(R²·C²) because of the multi-source seeding?' — multi-source DOESN'T multiply the complexity. The total DFS work is bounded by the number of CELLS visited (each at most once per matrix), not by the number of SEEDS. Seeds just determine where the work starts; the visited-matrix gate ensures work doesn't repeat.

If you wanted to extend to 'BFS instead of DFS' — same algorithm, swap the recursion for an explicit queue. Same O(R·C); avoids the stack-overflow risk on huge grids.

If you wanted to extend to 'cells that reach AT LEAST K of N oceans' (generalized to N edges/colors) — same template, N visited matrices, final loop counts which cells appear in ≥K. The structure generalizes cleanly.

The same multi-source reverse-flood template shows up in Walls and Gates (multi-source BFS from every gate to find shortest-distance-to-nearest-gate for each empty room), 01-Matrix (multi-source BFS from every 0 to find distance-to-nearest-0), and Rotting Oranges (multi-source BFS from rotten oranges spreading rot outward over time). The trick across all of them: reframe 'from each X, what's the answer?' as 'from the goal/source/target, flood OUT' — O(N·M) total instead of O((N·M)²) per-cell."
sections.why: The 'multi-source doesn't multiply complexity' argument is the textbook defense, and it's the question interviewers most often pull on — 'you have 2(R+C) starting points; isn't that 2(R+C)·R·C?' The answer is no: the visited gate bounds the total work to 2·R·C across all seeds. The Walls and Gates / 01-Matrix / Rotting Oranges cross-reference is the killer pattern recognition — those problems LOOK different (shortest distance, time-to-rot) but use the same multi-source-flood-outward-from-the-goal restructuring, and naming them proves you see Pacific Atlantic as one instance of a broader family rather than a clever one-off.

walkthrough.intro: Step through the reverse-flood DFS. Two visited grids — one per ocean — fill from the edge cells inward, only climbing to neighbors with equal-or-greater height. The answer is the row-major intersection.
trace: yield { line: 1, label: `enter pacificAtlantic — ${R}x${C} grid`, state: { heights } };
const pac = Array.from({ length: R }, () => new Array(C).fill(false));
const atl = Array.from({ length: R }, () => new Array(C).fill(false));
yield { line: 5, label: 'init pac + atl visited grids (all false)', state: { heights, pac: pac.map(r => [...r]), atl: atl.map(r => [...r]) } };
if (r < 0 || r >= R || c < 0 || c >= C) return;
yield { line: 18, label: `seed Pacific top row (0,${c}) + Atlantic bottom row (${R - 1},${c})`, state: { heights, pac: pac.map(r => [...r]), atl: atl.map(r => [...r]), edgeCol: c } };
yield { line: 18, label: 'top + bottom edges flooded', state: { heights, pac: pac.map(r => [...r]), atl: atl.map(r => [...r]) } };
yield { line: 19, label: `seed Pacific left col (${r},0) + Atlantic right col (${r},${C - 1})`, state: { heights, pac: pac.map(rw => [...rw]), atl: atl.map(rw => [...rw]), edgeRow: r } };
yield { line: 19, label: 'left + right edges flooded — both grids fully populated', state: { heights, pac: pac.map(r => [...r]), atl: atl.map(r => [...r]) } };
yield { line: 21, label: `(${r},${c}) reaches BOTH oceans — push`, state: { heights, pac: pac.map(rw => [...rw]), atl: atl.map(rw => [...rw]), out: out.map(p => [...p]) } };
yield { line: 22, label: `return ${JSON.stringify(out)}`, state: { out, returns: JSON.stringify(out) } };

notes: Flood is REVERSED: start at ocean edges and climb to cells with height >= current — that mirrors water flowing FROM a cell TO the ocean.
Two separate visited grids (one per ocean) so the same cell can be explored once per ocean — intersect at the end.
Top + left edges touch the Pacific; bottom + right edges touch the Atlantic — corners belong to both.

alternates.label: BFS multi-source (iterative queue)
alternates.when: Use BFS when you want to avoid recursion-stack overflow on large grids — a 200x200 grid with a tall mountain ridge can produce O(R*C) DFS depth. BFS uses an explicit queue and is otherwise structurally identical: same two visited grids, same reverse-climb rule, same intersection step.
notes: Mark each seed cell visited BEFORE pushing to the queue — prevents re-enqueuing edge cells when they appear in both the row and column seed loops (e.g., corners).
The BFS helper is a reusable function called twice — cleaner than duplicating the seeding logic for each ocean.
BFS explores level-by-level (by distance from edge) vs DFS depth-first; the reachability sets and output are identical.

questions.q: Why do we DFS from the ocean edges INWARD instead of from every cell outward?
options: Outward DFS produces wrong answers on plateaus because equal-height cells get visited twice
It is O(R*C) instead of O((R*C)^2) — each cell is visited at most twice total
Inward DFS lets a single visited grid serve both oceans, halving memory
Outward DFS cannot distinguish Pacific reachability from Atlantic reachability without a separate ocean ID per cell

questions.q: Reverse-flow rule from a neighbor with height `prev` into current cell with height `h`:
options: h > prev (strict — equal heights block reverse climb just as plateaus block natural flow)
abs(h - prev) <= 1 (water climbs only one elevation step at a time)

questions.q: Which edges seed the Pacific flood?
options: Only the top-left corner — the DFS propagates to the rest of the Pacific edge

questions.q: How is the final answer built?
options: Symmetric difference: cells reachable in exactly one of the two grids
Intersection: cells reachable in BOTH grids
Cells whose pac[r][c] index is greater than their atl[r][c] index

exercises.prompt: Fill in the reverse-flood Pacific/Atlantic DFS.

blanks.hint: reverse-flow comparator: stop when current is lower than prev

L3.prompt: Write `pacificAtlantic(heights)` — return all cells whose water can drain to BOTH oceans (Pacific = top + left edge, Atlantic = bottom + right). Use reverse DFS from each ocean. Log `JSON.stringify(result)` on the classic 5x5 example.
hints: Seed two DFS frontiers — one per ocean — at the edge cells.
Inside DFS, only continue when heights[neighbor] >= heights[current] (reverse flow).
Answer is the intersection of the two visited grids; iterate row-major to keep output sorted.
